pos: n. (a particular commandment or charge; rendering Hebrew piqqud, tsav, Greek entole)
etymology: From Latin praeceptum, from praecipere, to take beforehand, to instruct. A precept is a specific charge rather than a general principle — the particular, applied form of the law.
biblical_def: A precept is a particular charge laid on a particular people, and Psalm 119 makes it one of its eight words for the law of God. The psalmist states the manner as well as the fact: “Thou hast commanded us to keep thy precepts diligently” (Psalm 119:4) — not approximately, not in spirit only, but diligently. He then claims something more than obedience: “Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way” (Psalm 119:104). The order is worth marking, because it reverses the modern assumption. Understanding is not the precondition of obedience but its fruit; a man learns why God's way is right by walking in it, and the fruit of that understanding is not neutrality toward error but hatred of it. Isaiah gives the word its most quoted and most abused setting: “precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little” (Isaiah 28:10). And Jeremiah uses the word for a human father's charge with startling approval: the Rechabites had kept the precepts of Jonadab their father for generations, and God holds up their fidelity to a dead ancestor as a rebuke to Judah's infidelity to a living God (Jeremiah 35:18).
webster_summary: A particular charge. Psalm 119 requires precepts kept diligently and says understanding comes through them rather than before them; Isaiah 28:10 is the famous line-upon-line text; Jeremiah commends the Rechabites for keeping their father's precepts.
webster_full: PRECEPT, n. [L. praeceptum, from praecipio, to command; prae and capio.] In a general sense, any commandment or order intended as an authoritative rule of action.
2. In morality or religion, a commandment; a mandate; a rule directing moral conduct.
3. In law, a command or mandate in writing.
4. Doctrine; teaching; instruction; as the precepts of a master.
PRECEPTIVE, a. Containing precepts; giving rules or directions; didactic.
scriptures: Thou hast commanded us to keep thy precepts diligently.
Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way.
For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little:

And Jeremiah said unto the house of the Rechabites, Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Because ye have obeyed the commandment of Jonadab your father, and kept all his precepts, and done according unto all that he hath commanded you:
corruption_summary: Isaiah 28:10 is quoted as a positive method of Bible study — build doctrine line upon line — when in its own context it is the mocking speech of drunken scoffers imitating the prophet's tedious repetition, and God turns it back on them as judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: “Precept upon precept, line upon line” has furnished the title of Bible-study curricula and the motto of careful exposition, and the method it is used to commend is a good one. The verse itself is not commending it. Isaiah 28 opens with the drunkards of Ephraim; verse 9 asks contemptuously whom this prophet thinks he is teaching — children just weaned? — and verse 10 is the scoffers' mimicry of his preaching, a sing-song of baby-talk syllables in the Hebrew (tsav latsav, qav laqav). God's answer in verse 11 is that since they will not hear plain Hebrew, He will speak to them with stammering lips and another tongue — the Assyrian invader. The verse is a judgment on men who found God's word tediously elementary. That is a sharper word for the church than the study-method reading, and it is the one the text actually gives.

The deeper matter is what Psalm 119:104 says about how understanding is acquired. The modern instinct is to withhold obedience until the reason is clear: I will submit when I am persuaded. The psalmist reports the reverse order — through thy precepts I get understanding — and the Lord Jesus states it as a principle: if any man will do His will, he shall know of the doctrine (John 7:17). This is not anti-intellectualism; Psalm 119 is a long, deliberate meditation by a man who plainly thought hard. It is the claim that moral knowledge is not acquired at a distance, and that a man who will not keep the precepts he already understands will not be given more.
roots_summary: Hebrew piqqud (a precept, charge appointed, from paqad, to visit or appoint) and tsav (an injunction); Greek entole (a commandment) and entalma (a precept, used of the commandments of men).
roots_lines: Hebrew piqqud (H6490) — a precept, appointed charge; occurs 24 times, 21 of them in Psalm 119.
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, appoint, muster; the root, giving the precept its sense of something officially charged.
Hebrew tsav (H6673) — an injunction, precept; the word mimicked in Isaiah 28:10.
Greek entole (G1785) — a commandment, precept; the standard New Testament term.
Greek entalma (G1778) — a precept, injunction; used only of the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9; Colossians 2:22).
usage: “Keep thy precepts diligently” — the manner is commanded along with the matter.
“Through thy precepts I get understanding” — understanding is the fruit of obedience, not its precondition.
“Precept upon precept” — in context, the scoffers' mimicry of a prophet they found tedious.

pos: n. (an assembly convened for deliberation or judgment; rendering Greek synedrion)
etymology: From Latin concilium, an assembly called together. It is a different word from counsel (Latin consilium, advice), and the KJV keeps them distinct — a council is a body, counsel is what it gives.
biblical_def: In the Gospels a council is almost always the Sanhedrin, the seventy-member supreme court of the Jews, and the New Testament's portrait of it is a study in the failure of a lawful institution. The Lord Jesus assumes its authority as ordinary in the Sermon on the Mount, ranking it among real jurisdictions: whoever says Raca to his brother “shall be in danger of the council” (Matthew 5:22). John records the meeting at which it decides His death on frankly political grounds — “Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What do we? for this man doeth many miracles” (John 11:47) — where the miracles are not disputed but treated as a problem. Mark records the trial itself in a sentence that convicts the court rather than the prisoner: “the chief priests and all the council sought for witness against Jesus to put him to death; and found none” (Mark 14:55). A body that seeks witness in order to reach a verdict already decided has ceased to be a court. Acts then shows the same council examining the apostles and being obliged to send them out while it confers, unable to deny the healing done (Acts 4:15). The word passed into church usage for the great ecumenical assemblies — Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon — whose creeds the dictionary affirms without reservation.
webster_summary: An assembly for deliberation or judgment — in the Gospels, the Sanhedrin. It decides Christ's death over undisputed miracles, seeks witness to justify a verdict already reached, and cannot deny the apostles' healing.
webster_full: COUNCIL, n. [L. concilium.] An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
2. A body of men specially designated to advise a chief magistrate in the administration of the government.
3. An assembly of prelates and doctors, convened for regulating matters of doctrine and discipline in the church.
4. The great council of the Jews was called the Sanhedrim, consisting of seventy elders.
5. Act of deliberation; consultation of a council. Council is not to be confounded with counsel, advice.
scriptures: And the chief priests and all the council sought for witness against Jesus to put him to death; and found none.
Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What do we? for this man doeth many miracles.

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
But when they had commanded them to go aside out of the council, they conferred among themselves,
corruption_summary: Church councils are treated either as infallible — binding the conscience alongside Scripture — or as worthless, so that a Christian may hold Nicaea and Chalcedon as optional opinions; both errors misplace where authority actually sits.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome resolves the question of authority by locating infallibility in the church's councils and its head, so that conciliar definitions bind the conscience with the force of Scripture. The New Testament's own portrait of the highest council available — a lawfully constituted body, with genuine authority, condemning the Son of God on procured testimony — is a permanent argument against the premise. So is the record of church councils since: assemblies have contradicted one another, and the Second Council of Ephesus in 449 was so disgraceful that history calls it the Robber Synod. The confessional position is stated plainly in the 1689: councils and synods may err, and many have erred; therefore they are not to be made the rule of faith, but a help in both.

The opposite error is now more common among evangelicals: since councils can err, they may be ignored, and each believer works out the doctrine of the Trinity from his own reading. The result is a steady rediscovery of ancient heresies by men who have never heard their names — modalism preached from pulpits as an illustration of the Trinity, subordinationism defended as biblical, the two natures of Christ blurred in ordinary devotional speech. Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon are not a second canon; they are the church's accumulated reading of the canon at the points where it was tested hardest, and a man who sets them aside is not being more biblical than the fathers, only less instructed. The dictionary affirms those four councils and their creeds without reservation, as subordinate standards under Scripture alone.
roots_summary: Greek synedrion (a sitting together, hence a council — the Sanhedrin); Hebrew has no exact equivalent, though sod (a confidential council) is used of God's own assembly in Psalm 89:7 and Jeremiah 23:18.
roots_lines: Greek synedrion (G4892) — a council, the Sanhedrin; from syn (together) and hedra (a seat).
Greek symboulion (G4824) — a consultation, plan taken in council; the word in Matthew 12:14 and 27:1.
Hebrew sod (H5475) — a council, intimate circle; used of the counsel of the LORD in Jeremiah 23:18, which the false prophets never stood in.
Hebrew edah (H5712) — a congregation, assembly; the Old Testament gathering with judicial functions.
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly called out; the church's own word, distinct from synedrion.
usage: “Sought for witness… and found none” — a court seeking testimony to support a verdict already reached.
“What do we? for this man doeth many miracles” — the miracles undisputed and treated as a problem.
“Commanded them to go aside out of the council” — the highest court in Israel, conferring in private about a healing it cannot deny.

pos: v.t. (to pronounce judicially guilty and sentence; rendering Hebrew rasha in the causative, Greek katakrino)
etymology: From Latin condemnare, from con, intensive, and damnare, to sentence. The Greek katakrino is built the same way — kata, against, and krino, to judge: judgment given against.
biblical_def: To condemn is to pronounce guilty and sentence, and the New Testament's handling of the word is one of its glories. John states the purpose of the incarnation negatively first: “God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved” (John 3:17) — though the next verse is equally plain that he that believeth not is condemned already, so the sending is not condemnation because the condemnation was in place before He came. Paul opens the eighth chapter of Romans with the verdict that follows justification: “There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1), and closes the same chapter by daring anyone to reopen the case: “Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us” (Romans 8:34). The only qualified condemner is the one who died for the accused and is presently pleading for him. The Lord Jesus applies the word to the woman taken in adultery in the sentence that has been more misused than almost any other: “Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more” (John 8:11), where the pardon and the command are one utterance. And He warns that speech itself is evidence: “by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned” (Matthew 12:37).
webster_summary: To pronounce guilty and sentence. Christ came not to condemn the world but to save it; there is now no condemnation to those in Christ, and the only one qualified to condemn is the one who died and intercedes; and neither do I condemn thee is spoken with sin no more.
webster_full: CONDEMN, v.t. [L. condemno; con and damno, to condemn.] To pronounce to be utterly wrong; to utter a sentence of disapprobation against.
2. To determine or judge to be wrong, or guilty; to disallow.
3. To witness against; to show or prove to be wrong, or guilty, by a contrary practice.
4. To pronounce to be guilty; to sentence to punishment; to utter sentence against judicially.
5. To doom or sentence to pay a fine; to fine. There is now no condemnation. Rom. 8.
scriptures: There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.
Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth.
For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved.
She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.
corruption_summary: “Neither do I condemn thee” is quoted without “go, and sin no more,” making Christ the patron of moral indifference — and judge not is deployed alongside it to forbid any moral assessment whatever.
corruption_paragraphs: The half-verse from John 8 has become the most-cited sentence of Jesus in public argument, and it is nearly always severed from its second clause. The Lord Jesus says both things in one breath: no condemnation, and no more sin. Remove the second and He becomes indifferent to adultery; remove the first and He becomes her accuser. The scene also refutes the use it is put to in another way — the accusers were not wrong that the law condemned her, and Christ never says they were. He says the executioner must be without sin, and He alone qualified and declined. Then He sends her away free and changed. That is precisely the gospel: the condemnation was real, it fell elsewhere, and the pardoned sinner is commanded to leave the sin behind.

“Judge not, that ye be not judged” is the companion text, and Matthew 7 continues past the slogan. The passage forbids hypocritical judgment — the beam and the mote — and its remedy is not to abandon the assessment but to remove the beam and then see clearly to cast out the mote (Matthew 7:5). Six verses later the same sermon requires discriminating between swine and holy things, and shortly after that between false prophets and true by their fruits, which is judgment of a demanding kind. The New Testament forbids condemnation, which is the passing of final sentence on a soul, and requires discernment, which is the ordinary work of a Christian conscience. Confusing the two has left many congregations unable to say anything at all, which is not humility but abdication.
roots_summary: Hebrew rasha in the hiphil (to declare wicked, condemn); Greek katakrino (to judge against, condemn) and katakrima (the sentence of condemnation, the noun in Romans 8:1).
roots_lines: Hebrew rasha (H7561) — in the causative, to declare guilty, condemn; the opposite of tsadaq, to declare righteous.
Greek katakrino (G2632) — to give judgment against, condemn; the verb in Romans 8:34 and John 8:11.
Greek katakrima (G2631) — the sentence of condemnation; the noun in Romans 5:16, 18 and 8:1.
Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, decide; the neutral root, from which both discernment and condemnation are formed.
Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, justify; the forensic opposite, and the reason condemnation is a courtroom word.
usage: “There is therefore now no condemnation” — a verdict, not a feeling, and grounded in justification.
“Who is he that condemneth?” — the only qualified condemner died for the accused and is pleading for him.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more” — one utterance, and it is generally quoted half.

pos: adj. (the same in measure, worth, or standing; also, fair and even-handed; rendering Hebrew takan, Greek isos)
etymology: From Latin aequalis, from aequus, level, even. The KJV carries both senses — identical in degree, as in Christ's equality with the Father, and even-handed, as in the masters' duty to render what is just and equal.
biblical_def: Equal in Scripture bears the full metaphysical weight in the Christological texts and a plain ethical weight elsewhere. Paul writes that Christ, “being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God” (Philippians 2:6) — equality with God was not something snatched at, because it was already His by right; and the humbling that follows is the more astonishing for it. John records the same claim from the hostile side, and the hostility proves the claim was understood: the Jews sought the more to kill Him “because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18). No one present treated this as a metaphor. In the ethical register, Paul lays a duty on masters that was revolutionary in a slaveholding empire: “Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1) — the ground being that the master is himself a servant. Ezekiel meets the complaint of a people who think God unfair: “Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. Hear now, O house of Israel; Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal?” (Ezekiel 18:25). And the parable of the labourers turns on the word: the first-hired object that the householder has made the last “equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day” (Matthew 20:12), and the answer is that no one was defrauded — grace given to another takes nothing from you.
webster_summary: The same in measure or standing, and also even-handed. Christ's equality with God is His by right; masters owe servants what is just and equal; Ezekiel answers those who call God's way unequal; and the labourers resent an equality that cost them nothing.
webster_full: EQUAL, a. [L. aequalis, from aequus, even, level.] Having the same magnitude or dimensions; being of the same bulk or extent.
2. Having the same value; being of the same importance.
3. Having the same qualities or condition; as, men are equal in their natural rights.
4. Even; uniform; not variable; as an equal temper.
5. Just; equitable; giving the same or similar rights or advantages. Give unto your servants that which is just and equal. Col. 4.
scriptures: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:
Therefore the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God.
Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven.
Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. Hear now, O house of Israel; Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal?
corruption_summary: Equality has been converted from a statement about worth and standing into a demand for identical outcomes, so that any difference of role, reward, or result is read as injustice — a premise Scripture answers directly in the parable of the labourers.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's equality is genuine and radical: every human being bears the image of God; the ground is level at the cross, where there is no difference, for all have sinned; and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female as to standing and inheritance. What Scripture never derives from that is the identity of roles or the equalisation of outcomes. The same apostle who wrote Galatians 3:28 assigned different offices in the household and the church; the same Lord who declared all men equally guilty distributed talents unequally, five and two and one, and required an account proportioned to what was given. The parable of the labourers is the decisive text because it stages the objection precisely: the complaint is not that anyone was underpaid but that others were treated generously, and the householder's answer is that his eye is good and theirs is evil. Envy dressed as a demand for fairness is an old vice with a new vocabulary.

The Christological texts are corrupted in the opposite direction and with graver consequence. Philippians 2:6 has been rendered so as to make Christ a man who declined to grasp at a divinity He did not possess, and John 5:18 dismissed as the Jews' misunderstanding — the standard route by which Arian and Unitarian readings dispose of the deity of Christ. Neither works. Paul's point requires that Christ already possessed what He did not clutch, or the emptying is empty. And John reports the charge without correcting it, then has Jesus answer at length in a way that heightens rather than reduces the claim: what things soever the Father doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise (John 5:19). The dictionary holds the Nicene confession that the Son is of one substance with the Father, equal in power and glory.
roots_summary: Hebrew takan (to weigh, measure, make even — the verb rendered equal in Ezekiel 18:25) and shavah (to be level, equal); Greek isos (equal) and isotes (equality, equity).
roots_lines: Hebrew takan (H8505) — to weigh out, measure, make even; the verb behind the way of the Lord is not equal.
Hebrew shavah (H7737) — to be level, equal, comparable; used in Proverbs 3:15 of nothing being comparable to wisdom.
Greek isos (G2470) — equal, the same; the word in Philippians 2:6, John 5:18, and Matthew 20:12.
Greek isotes (G2471) — equality, equity, fairness; the word in Colossians 4:1 and 2 Corinthians 8:13-14.
Greek harpagmos (G725) — a thing seized or to be grasped at; the noun rendered robbery in Philippians 2:6.
usage: “Thought it not robbery to be equal with God” — not snatched at, because already His by right.
“Making himself equal with God” — the charge is reported and never corrected.
“Thou hast made them equal unto us” — the complaint of men who lost nothing by another's generosity.

pos: n. (a valuation set by appraisal; rendering Hebrew erek, from arak, to arrange or set in order)
etymology: From Latin aestimatio, a valuing, from aestimare, to appraise. In Leviticus it is a technical term of the sanctuary: the fixed price at which a vowed person, animal, house, or field is redeemed.
biblical_def: Estimation is a technical term of Leviticus 27, the chapter that governs vows. When a man devoted a person to the LORD, the person was not surrendered but redeemed at a fixed valuation: “When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation” (Leviticus 27:2), with a published scale following by age and sex. The scale is the ancient counterpart of a schedule of fees, and it does two things at once. It prevents the vow from becoming human sacrifice — Israel's neighbours devoted children to their gods, and this legislation makes a devoted person a redeemed person. And it prevents the vow from becoming a device of the rich, because the chapter includes a means test: “if he be poorer than thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest shall value him; according to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him” (Leviticus 27:8). The poor man is not excused from his vow and not crushed by it; the priest sets a price he can pay. The firstborn are redeemed on the same principle at a fixed five shekels (Numbers 18:16), the price Mary and Joseph would have reckoned with. Behind the whole apparatus is a truth the New Testament makes explicit: persons belong to God, and what belongs to God is bought back rather than given up.
webster_summary: A fixed valuation for redeeming what was vowed. Leviticus 27 publishes a scale so that a devoted person is redeemed rather than surrendered, and adds a means test so the poor man's vow is priced to his ability.
webster_full: ESTIMATION, n. [L. aestimatio.] The act of estimating.
2. Calculation; computation; an adjusting of numbers or value.
3. Value; as, a thing of no estimation.
4. Esteem; regard; favorable opinion; honor.
5. In the Mosaic law, the valuation set by the priest upon persons or things devoted by vow. Lev. 27.
scriptures: Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation.
But if he be poorer than thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest shall value him; according to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him.
And those that are to be redeemed from a month old shalt thou redeem, according to thine estimation, for the money of five shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary, which is twenty gerahs.
And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land, or of the fruit of the tree, is the LORD'S: it is the LORD'S holy.
corruption_summary: The valuation scale of Leviticus 27 is read as Scripture assigning different human worth by age and sex — a misreading of a redemption tariff as a statement of value, and one that ignores what the chapter is actually preventing.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection is raised often: Leviticus 27 prices a man at fifty shekels and a woman at thirty, therefore Scripture values women at three-fifths of a man. The chapter is not appraising souls; it is setting a redemption tariff for vows, and the figures track the market value of labour in an agrarian economy, which is why they also vary by age — a man over sixty is valued below a man in his prime, and an infant lowest of all. No one supposes Scripture holds the elderly to be worth less than the young as persons; the same chapter that prices them is in the book that commands rising before the hoary head. The theological valuation is stated elsewhere and without gradation: male and female alike created in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and both redeemed at the same price, which is not silver or gold but the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19).

What the chapter is actually doing is worth more attention than the objection. Israel lived among nations that devoted children to their gods in the literal sense; Leviticus makes the devotion of a person into a monetary redemption, which is why Jephthah's vow is narrated as a horror rather than a model — the law had provided him a way out he did not take. And verse 8 builds in a provision most modern legislation lacks: an obligation scaled to ability, assessed case by case by a priest who must look at the man in front of him. The rich man pays the published rate and the poor man pays what he can, and both have kept their vow. That is a more careful piece of equity than the passage's critics usually credit.
roots_summary: Hebrew erek (an arrangement, valuation, estimate) from arak (to set in order, arrange, lay out); the Greek Old Testament renders it time, price or honour — the same word behind the New Testament's bought with a price.
roots_lines: Hebrew erek (H6187) — an arrangement, estimate, valuation; the technical term throughout Leviticus 27.
Hebrew arak (H6186) — to arrange, set in order, lay out; used of setting the shewbread and of drawing up an army.
Hebrew ga'al (H1350) and padah (H6299) — to redeem, ransom; the two verbs governing what is done with a valued thing.
Greek time (G5092) — price, value, honour; the Septuagint's rendering, and the word in 1 Corinthians 6:20.
Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a devoted thing; the category in Leviticus 27:28-29 that, unlike a vow, could not be redeemed.
usage: “The persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation” — a devoted person is redeemed, not surrendered.
“According to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him” — an obligation scaled to means, assessed case by case.
“For the money of five shekels” — the fixed redemption of the firstborn.

pos: n. (a total, the whole of a reckoning; also the substance or gist of a matter; rendering Hebrew rosh, Greek kephalaion)
etymology: From Latin summa, the top, the highest — because Roman accountants added upward and wrote the total at the head of the column. Both Hebrew rosh and Greek kephalaion likewise mean head, so all three languages call a total the head of the reckoning.
biblical_def: A sum is a total, and the word carries both an arithmetical and a rhetorical sense in Scripture. Arithmetically, taking the sum of Israel is the census, and it comes with an unexpected requirement: “When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the LORD” (Exodus 30:12) — counting the people is dangerous, because a census is a reckoning of a strength that is not the king's, and David learned the danger the hard way. The half-shekel ransom acknowledges that every counted man is a redeemed man. Luke gives a memorable commercial use: the chief captain, hearing Paul claim Roman citizenship, says “With a great sum obtained I this freedom” — and Paul answers, “But I was free born” (Acts 22:28), an exchange in which purchased status meets birthright, and which every Christian may read twice over. The psalmist uses the word for something uncountable: “How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! how great is the sum of them!” (Psalm 139:17). And Hebrews uses the rhetorical sense to head its central argument: “Now of the things which we have spoken this is the sum: We have such an high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens” (Hebrews 8:1) — the whole epistle reduced to one clause.
webster_summary: A total, and the substance of a matter. The census sum requires a ransom for every counted man; a Roman captain bought his citizenship with a great sum where Paul was free born; and Hebrews heads its central argument with this is the sum.
webster_full: SUM, n. [L. summa, from summus, highest.] The aggregate of two or more numbers, magnitudes, quantities or particulars; the amount or whole of any number of individuals or particulars added.
2. A quantity of money or currency; any amount indefinitely.
3. Compendium; abridgment; the amount; the substance.
4. Height; completion.
SUM, v.t. To add particulars into one whole; to collect two or more particular numbers into one number.
scriptures: When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the LORD, when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them.
And the chief captain answered, With a great sum obtained I this freedom. And Paul said, But I was free born.
How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! how great is the sum of them!
Now of the things which we have spoken this is the sum: We have such an high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens;
corruption_summary: The instinct to measure a work of God by its totals — attendance, giving, converts counted — repeats the sin of David's census, in which numbering a strength that belongs to God became an act of self-congratulation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself; the corruption is a practice rather than a lexical shift. Exodus 30:12 attaches a ransom to every census, and 2 Samuel 24 records what happens when a king numbers his people without one: David's heart smote him afterward, and Joab — not a tender man — had tried to talk him out of it. The problem is not arithmetic. Scripture counts constantly; the fourth book of the Bible is named for a census. The problem is a reckoning undertaken to measure one's own strength, which turns God's gift into an inventory of assets. The modern equivalent is not hard to identify: the ministry report in which numbers do the work that faithfulness should, the pastor who knows his attendance to the person and his congregation's sins not at all, the denominational statistic that decides which churches are serious. Counting is lawful; counting in order to be impressed is the census sin.

The principle to recover is the one Hebrews 8:1 models. When the writer says this is the sum, he is not totalling results but stating substance: we have such an high priest. That is the reckoning by which a church should be measured — what it has in Christ and what it holds of the truth — and it does not vary with the attendance. Psalm 139 supplies the counterweight from the other side: God's thoughts toward His people are more in number than the sand, a sum no one is asked to total. The man who is content to be numbered among a people he cannot count, by a God whose thoughts toward him he cannot count either, has escaped the temptation entirely.
roots_summary: Hebrew rosh (head, and so a total — lift up the head is the idiom for taking a census); Greek kephalaion (the chief point, sum) from kephale, head; Latin summa, the top.
roots_lines: Hebrew rosh (H7218) — head, top, sum; in the idiom nasa rosh, to lift the head, meaning to take a census.
Hebrew miphqad (H4662) — a mustering, numbering; the term for the census in 2 Samuel 24:9.
Greek kephalaion (G2774) — the chief point, main thing, sum; the word in Hebrews 8:1 and Acts 22:28.
Greek kephale (G2776) — head; the root, which is why a total is called a sum in three languages.
Hebrew kopher (H3724) — a ransom, covering price; the half-shekel required of every man counted in Exodus 30:12.
usage: “When thou takest the sum… then shall they give every man a ransom” — every counted man is a redeemed man.
“With a great sum obtained I this freedom… But I was free born” — purchased status meets birthright.
“This is the sum: We have such an high priest” — a whole epistle reduced to one clause.

pos: n. and v.t. (a stock laid up; to lay up in reserve; rendering Hebrew otsar, micken, Greek thesaurizo, apothesaurizo)
etymology: From Old French estor, from Latin instaurare, to restore or provide. Scripture's attitude to a store is not simple — Joseph's granaries save a world, and the rich fool's barns damn a man, and the difference is not in the quantity.
biblical_def: To lay up in store is to set aside a reserve, and Scripture treats the practice as good, dangerous, or commanded depending entirely on what the reserve is for. It is commanded for the poor: Paul's collection instruction is the New Testament's clearest word on systematic giving — “Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come” (1 Corinthians 16:2). Four things are in that sentence: giving is weekly, individual, proportionate to income, and planned rather than impulsive. It is commanded for eternity, and paradoxically the storing is done by giving away: the rich are charged to be rich in good works, ready to distribute, “Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold on eternal life” (1 Timothy 6:19). Under the old covenant the storehouse is the temple treasury, and Malachi's challenge is unique in Scripture for inviting a test: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith” (Malachi 3:10). And Joseph's store cities preserved Egypt and the covenant family through seven years of famine — providence working through an administrator with warehouses. Against all this stands the barn-building of Luke 12, where a man stores for himself and is not rich toward God.
webster_summary: A reserve laid up, good or damning depending on its end. Paul commands weekly, proportionate laying-by for the poor; Timothy's rich lay up a foundation by giving away; Malachi invites a test at the storehouse; and the rich fool builds barns for himself.
webster_full: STORE, n. [Old Fr. estor.] A large number or quantity; a great plenty; abundance.
2. A stock provided; a large quantity collected for supply; hence, abundance.
3. A store-house; a magazine; a warehouse.
STORE, v.t. To furnish; to supply; to replenish.
4. To lay up in store; to reposit in a store or warehouse for preservation. Lay by him in store. 1 Cor. 16.
scriptures: Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come.
Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold on eternal life.

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.
corruption_summary: Malachi 3:10 has been made the engine of a giving-to-get transaction, in which the tithe is an investment with a promised return — while 1 Corinthians 16:2, the plainer and more demanding text, is rarely preached at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Malachi 3:10 is the prosperity movement's foundational text, and its use there inverts the passage. The chapter is an indictment: a nation is robbing God by withholding tithes and offerings, and is under a curse for it. The invitation to prove God is the offer of restored covenant blessing to a repentant people, framed in the agricultural terms of Deuteronomy 28 — rain in season, the devourer rebuked, the vine not casting her fruit. It is not a formula by which any individual may treat God as a fund manager. The corruption is exposed by what it asks: a man who gives in order to receive has not given at all, and the arrangement makes God a debtor, which Romans 11:35 flatly denies. The dictionary affirms generous, sacrificial, and proportionate giving as the plain duty of every Christian, and denies that God has promised a financial return on it.

The more interesting fact is which text goes unpreached. 1 Corinthians 16:2 is more demanding than the tithe-as-investment scheme in every respect, and it is largely absent from pulpits that quote Malachi weekly. It requires that giving be regular — the first day of every week; universal — every one of you, not merely the prosperous; proportionate — as God hath prospered him, so that the amount rises with income; and planned — laid by in advance, so that the offering is a decision made at the desk rather than an impulse in the pew. A congregation that adopted that verse alone would give more, more consistently, and with less manipulation than any appeal to Malachi has ever produced. And 1 Timothy 6:19 supplies the motive that keeps it from becoming mere duty: the storing that lasts is done by distributing.
roots_summary: Hebrew otsar (a treasury, storehouse) and miskenoth (store cities, as Pithom and Raamses); Greek thesaurizo (to lay up treasure) and apothesaurizo (to store away, the verb in 1 Timothy 6:19).
roots_lines: Hebrew otsar (H214) — a treasury, storehouse; the word in Malachi 3:10 and of the temple treasuries.
Hebrew miskenoth (H4543) — store cities, magazines; the cities Israel built for Pharaoh in Exodus 1:11.
Greek thesaurizo (G2343) — to lay up treasure, hoard; the verb in Matthew 6:19-20 and 1 Corinthians 16:2.
Greek apothesaurizo (G597) — to store away, treasure up for oneself; a hapax at 1 Timothy 6:19.
Greek euodoo (G2137) — to prosper, be led along a good road; the verb in 1 Corinthians 16:2 rendered as God hath prospered him.
usage: “Lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him” — weekly, individual, proportionate, and planned.
“Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation” — the storing is accomplished by the distributing.
“Prove me now herewith” — a covenant invitation to a repentant nation, not a formula for personal return.

pos: n. (wages due for work done; rendering Hebrew sakar, Greek misthos)
etymology: Old English hyr, wages. The biblical usage is almost entirely about timing and justice — not what a wage is but when it must be paid, and what happens when it is withheld.
biblical_def: A hire is wages earned, and Scripture's legislation about it is unusually urgent. The law requires same-day payment for the day labourer, and states the reason in human terms: “At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD, and it be sin unto thee” (Deuteronomy 24:15). The man is counting on that money for the evening meal; the employer who holds it overnight for his own convenience has taken food from a household, and the transaction is placed under God's ear. James takes up the same law against wealthy Christians and makes the wages themselves the plaintiff: “the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth” (James 5:4) — unpaid wages cry out like Abel's blood. On the other side, the Lord Jesus establishes that gospel labour is real labour deserving real pay: “the labourer is worthy of his hire” (Luke 10:7), and Paul cites that saying as scripture alongside Deuteronomy's unmuzzled ox (1 Timothy 5:18) — an early and remarkable indication that the Gospel words of Christ were already reckoned canonical.
webster_summary: Wages due. The law requires the day labourer paid before sundown because he is counting on it; James says withheld wages cry into God's ears; and Christ establishes that the gospel labourer is worthy of his hire.
webster_full: HIRE, v.t. [Sax. hyran.] To procure from another person and for temporary use, at a certain price, or for a stipulated or reasonable equivalent.
2. To engage in service for a stipulated reward; to contract with for a compensation; as, to hire a servant for a year.
HIRE, n. Wages; the price, reward or compensation paid or contracted to be given for the temporary use of a thing.
3. The reward or recompense paid for personal service. The laborer is worthy of his hire. Luke 10.
HIRELING, n. One who is hired, or who serves for wages; and hence, a mercenary, one who serves for reward only.
scriptures: At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD, and it be sin unto thee.

Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
And in the same house remain, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Go not from house to house.
For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.
corruption_summary: Luke 10:7 is stretched into a warrant for ministerial luxury, while the far more frequent biblical concern — wages withheld from working people — is treated as social commentary outside the church's proper business.
corruption_paragraphs: “The labourer is worthy of his hire” establishes a real and often neglected duty: churches ought to pay their ministers, and a congregation that keeps its pastor poor to keep him humble has misread both the text and human nature. Paul insists on the principle in 1 Corinthians 9 at length. But he insists on it while declining to use it, that he might make the gospel without charge, and he lists among an elder's qualifications that he be not greedy of filthy lucre (1 Timothy 3:3). The verse warrants a living, not an estate; and Peter's charge to feed the flock not for filthy lucre but of a ready mind (1 Peter 5:2) stands over every ministry whose finances would embarrass it if published. The Lord's own instruction in Luke 10 is notably modest — eat what is set before you, and do not shop for a better house.

The neglected half is the one Scripture presses hardest. Deuteronomy 24:15 and James 5:4 are about employers, and James is writing to a church. The sin named is not merely underpaying but delaying — keeping back what is owed, which in a day-labour economy meant a family went hungry that night, and which in a modern economy has its exact equivalents in slow payment to small contractors, misclassified workers, and wage theft that is cheaper to commit than to litigate. Scripture puts these cries in the ears of the Lord of sabaoth, the LORD of armies, which is a deliberately military title for a verse about payroll. A church that examines its members on doctrine and never on how they pay the people who work for them has an incomplete idea of what sin is.
roots_summary: Hebrew sakar (wages, hire) and sakir (a hired servant); Greek misthos (wages, reward) and misthios / misthotos (a hired servant, hireling).
roots_lines: Hebrew sakar (H7939) — wages, hire, reward; the word in Deuteronomy 24:15 and Genesis 15:1 (thy exceeding great reward).
Hebrew sakir (H7916) — a hired servant, day labourer; the class the law protects in Deuteronomy 24:14.
Greek misthos (G3408) — wages, hire, reward; the word in Luke 10:7 and James 5:4.
Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hireling; the man in John 10:12-13 who flees because the sheep are not his own.
Greek apostereo (G650) — to defraud, keep back by fraud; the verb in James 5:4.
usage: “Neither shall the sun go down upon it” — the day labourer is paid the same day, because he is counting on it.
“The hire of the labourers… crieth” — withheld wages are a plaintiff before the Lord of sabaoth.
“The labourer is worthy of his hire” — cited by Paul as scripture, alongside Deuteronomy.

pos: v.t. (to take another's property without right; rendering Hebrew ganab, Greek klepto)
etymology: Old English stelan. The eighth commandment's Hebrew ganab covers taking by stealth as distinct from robbery by force, and it is the root of the New Testament kleptes — a thief who comes unseen rather than a robber who comes armed.
biblical_def: The eighth commandment is two words in Hebrew and three in English: “Thou shalt not steal” (Exodus 20:15). Its brevity conceals how much it establishes. A commandment against theft presupposes property that can be stolen, and so Scripture's law code assumes and protects private ownership — a man's field, house, ox, and cloak are genuinely his, and the same law obliges him to leave gleanings, lend without usury to a poor brother, and release debts in the seventh year. Paul gives the commandment its full New Testament shape, which is not merely a prohibition but a reversal: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth” (Ephesians 4:28). The thief's repentance is a three-stage movement — stop taking, start working, and work in order to give — so that the man ends as a source where he began as a drain. Agur's prayer supplies the pastoral realism, asking for neither poverty nor riches because each has its own temptation: “Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain” (Proverbs 30:9). And the Lord Jesus identifies theft as the mark of the false shepherd: the thief cometh not but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy (John 10:10).
webster_summary: To take what is another's. The eighth commandment presupposes and protects real property; Paul turns the thief into a giver by way of work; Agur prays against both riches and poverty because each has its own temptation to theft.
webster_full: STEAL, v.t. [Sax. stelan.] To take and carry away feloniously, as the personal goods of another. To constitute stealing, the taking must be felonious, that is, with an intent to take what belongs to another, and without his consent.
2. To withdraw or convey without notice or clandestinely.
3. To gain or win by address or gradual and imperceptible means; as, to steal the affections.
STEAL, v.i. To withdraw or pass privily; to slip along or away unperceived.
5. To practice theft; to take feloniously. Thou shalt not steal. Ex. 20.
scriptures: Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.
The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
corruption_summary: Theft is redefined by category — taking from the wealthy, from a corporation, or from the state is reclassified as recovery or protest — and in the opposite direction, the commandment is treated as though it protected property absolutely, with no obligation attached to its use.
corruption_paragraphs: The most common modern erosion of the eighth commandment is jurisdictional: the thing taken is said not to be really owned, or the owner said not to deserve it, and the taking becomes redistribution, shrinkage, or a blow struck against a system. Scripture recognises no such exemption. It does insist, relentlessly, that the wealthy owe the poor — gleanings, interest-free loans, the seventh-year release, prompt wages, open-handedness — but it establishes those as duties on the owner, not as licences for the taker. The distinction matters practically: a duty enforced by conscience and community produces generosity, and a licence to take produces a society in which nothing is secure and the poor suffer first, since they have the least margin and the least protection. Zacchaeus is Scripture's model of a rich man converted, and his restitution is fourfold and voluntary.

The mirror error belongs to those who quote the commandment as a full theory of property. It is not. The same law that says thou shalt not steal says the land shall not be sold for ever, for the land is mine (Leviticus 25:23), and every Israelite held his field as a tenant of God on a fifty-year lease. Ownership in Scripture is real, protected, and derivative — a stewardship rather than an absolute dominion — which is why the same chapter that protects the field also commands its corners be left unharvested. And Ephesians 4:28 gives the commandment its evangelical form: the aim is not merely a man who no longer steals but a man who works in order to have something to give. That is more than restitution; it is the direction of a life reversed.
roots_summary: Hebrew ganab (to steal, take by stealth) and gannab (a thief); Greek klepto (to steal) and kleptes (a thief), distinct from lestes, a robber or bandit who uses force.
roots_lines: Hebrew ganab (H1589) — to steal, carry away by stealth; the verb of the eighth commandment.
Hebrew gannab (H1590) — a thief; the offender whose restitution is set out in Exodus 22:1-4.
Greek klepto (G2813) — to steal; the verb in Ephesians 4:28 and Matthew 6:19-20.
Greek kleptes (G2812) — a thief, one who takes by stealth; the word in John 10:10 and 1 Thessalonians 5:2.
Greek lestes (G3027) — a robber, bandit using violence; the word for Barabbas and for the two crucified with Christ.
usage: “Thou shalt not steal” — three words that presuppose real property and a real owner.
“Let him labour… that he may have to give” — the thief's repentance ends in generosity, not merely in restraint.
“Lest I be poor, and steal” — Agur prays against both riches and poverty, naming the temptation of each.

pos: v.t. (to crush or burden by unjust use of power; rendering Hebrew ashaq, lachats, yanah, Greek katadynasteuo)
etymology: From Latin opprimere, to press against or crush — ob, against, and premere, to press. The Hebrew ashaq carries the same physical sense of weight brought down on someone who cannot lift it off.
biblical_def: To oppress is to use power against those who have none, and Scripture names four standing categories of the vulnerable and forbids their oppression together: “oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart” (Zechariah 7:10). The list is not sentimental but structural — each of the four lacked a male protector, a landholding, or legal standing in an agrarian society, and the law repeatedly attaches God Himself as their advocate. The theological ground is stated in a proverb that makes economic conduct a matter of theology proper: “He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor” (Proverbs 14:31). To grind a poor man is to insult the God whose image he bears. The law forbids it specifically of employees — “Thou shalt not oppress an hired servant that is poor and needy, whether he be of thy brethren, or of thy strangers that are in thy land within thy gates” (Deuteronomy 24:14) — with the stranger included on the same terms as the brother. Ecclesiastes records the bleakest observation in the canon on the subject: “behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter” (Ecclesiastes 4:1). And James, writing to churches, asks the pointed question: do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats? (James 2:6).
webster_summary: To crush by unjust power. Scripture names the widow, fatherless, stranger, and poor as the standing objects of protection; oppressing the poor reproaches their Maker; Ecclesiastes records the oppressed having no comforter; James asks the church whose side it is taking.
webster_full: OPPRESS, v.t. [L. oppressus, from opprimo; ob and premo, to press.] To load or burden with unreasonable impositions; to treat with unjust severity, rigor or hardship.
2. To overpower; to overburden; as, to be oppressed with grief.
3. To sit heavy on; to lie heavily upon.
OPPRESSION, n. The act of oppressing; cruelty; severity; unjust hardship imposed on inferiors.
4. A sense of heaviness or weight in the body or mind; dullness; depression.
scriptures: And oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart.
He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor.
Thou shalt not oppress an hired servant that is poor and needy, whether he be of thy brethren, or of thy strangers that are in thy land within thy gates:

So I returned, and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter.
corruption_summary: Oppression has been converted from an act into an identity — a permanent status assigned by group membership rather than a wrong done by a person to a person — which makes the biblical categories unrecognisable and the biblical remedy impossible.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's doctrine of oppression is concrete: someone with power did something to someone without it, and both are named. The widow whose field was seized, the labourer whose wage was withheld, the stranger denied justice at the gate — these are acts with agents, victims, and remedies, and the law provides courts, restitution, and gleaning rights. The framework that has replaced it in much public and increasingly church discourse assigns oppressor and oppressed by category, so that guilt attaches to a group and innocence to another, independent of what any individual has done. The Bible's anthropology forbids this at the root: all are one in Adam and equally guilty (Romans 5:12), all who are in Christ are one in Him (Galatians 3:28), and the courts of Israel were forbidden to favour either the mighty or the poor but to judge the case (Leviticus 19:15). A category cannot repent, cannot make restitution, and cannot be forgiven; only a person can, which is why the substitution costs the church its actual remedy.

The opposite failure is at least as common and is committed by many who see the first one clearly. Having rejected the fashionable framework, conservative churches frequently drop the subject altogether, as though the prophets' sustained attention to withheld wages, false balances, bribed judges, and devoured widows' houses were a liberal preoccupation. It is not; it is most of Amos, much of Isaiah, and a good deal of James. Proverbs 14:31 makes how a man treats the poor a statement about how he regards God. The dictionary holds both: oppression is real, God hates it, and He hears the cry of the oppressed — and the account of it must be the biblical one, in which persons wrong persons, God is the advocate of the wronged, and the remedy runs through repentance, restitution, and just courts rather than through the reassignment of guilt by category.
roots_summary: Hebrew ashaq (to oppress, defraud, extort), lachats (to squeeze, press), and yanah (to vex, mistreat — used especially of the stranger); Greek katadynasteuo (to exercise power down against).
roots_lines: Hebrew ashaq (H6231) — to oppress, defraud, extort; the verb in Proverbs 14:31 and Deuteronomy 24:14.
Hebrew lachats (H3905) — to squeeze, press, oppress; used of Egypt's treatment of Israel in Exodus 3:9.
Hebrew yanah (H3238) — to vex, mistreat; used especially of wronging the stranger (Exodus 22:21; Leviticus 19:33).
Hebrew ger (H1616) — a sojourner, stranger; one of the four standing categories under God's protection.
Greek katadynasteuo (G2616) — to exercise dominion against, oppress; the verb in James 2:6 and Acts 10:38.
usage: “The widow, the fatherless, the stranger, the poor” — the four standing categories, each lacking a protector.
“He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker” — economic conduct made a matter of theology proper.
“They had no comforter” — repeated twice in one verse; Ecclesiastes will not soften it.
